questions.stem: For a moving object, a resultant force produces:

options.text: A change in the object's mass
options.explanation: Forces change motion, not the amount of matter present.
Accelerating or decelerating a moving object is precisely a momentum change.

options.text: Nothing unless a collision takes place
options.explanation: Any resultant force on a moving object changes its momentum, collision or not.

options.text: A change of direction only, never of speed
options.explanation: A force can change speed as well as direction.

questions.stem: Combining F = ma with momentum p = mv over a contact time t gives:

options.explanation: The momentum terms subtract, because Δp is final minus initial.
That is the numerator alone; the division by time has been dropped.
Substituting a = (v − u)/t into F = ma and multiplying by m lands exactly here.
The contact time divides the change; multiplying is the inverse operation.

questions.stem: In the force equation, the change in momentum is measured in:

options.explanation: Momentum change is mass × velocity change, so its unit is kg m/s.
Newtons measure the force itself, not the momentum change inside it.
m/s belongs to each velocity, not to mass × velocity.
Kilograms measure mass alone.

questions.stem: In the force equation F = (mv − mu)/t, the letter u stands for:

options.explanation: u and v are swapped: u comes first in time.
Acceleration is a, from F = ma.
The momentum change is the whole numerator mv − mu, not one letter.
u is the initial velocity; v is the final one.

questions.stem: A ball bounces straight back along its original path. Taking the outward direction as positive, its return velocity is entered as:

options.explanation: Only motion along the chosen positive direction counts positive; the return leg runs the other way.
The return motion is opposite to the chosen positive direction, so its velocity enters as negative.
A rebounding ball is still moving fast; zero would mean instant rest.

options.text: Unsigned until a direction is declared
options.explanation: A direction has been declared here, and velocity always carries a sign in this equation.

questions.stem: State the equation that links force with the momentum change and the time, and give the unit of that momentum change.
questions.modelAnswer: F = (mv − mu)/t, with the force in newtons and the numerator mv − mu — the momentum change — in kg m/s.

questions.stem: Why must one direction be chosen as positive before velocities are substituted into the force equation?
questions.modelAnswer: Velocity is a vector, so motion in the reverse direction must be substituted as a negative value; without that sign convention the momentum change, and hence the force, comes out wrong.

questions.stem: Explain why a resultant force on a moving object changes its momentum.
questions.modelAnswer: A resultant force changes the object's velocity — speeding it up or slowing it down. Since momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, any velocity change must also change the momentum.

questions.stem: A 2 kg ball rolling at 6 m/s is brought to rest in 0.5 s. Taking its initial direction as positive, calculate the force on the ball.
questions.modelAnswer: mv = 2 × 0 = 0 and mu = 2 × 6 = 12 kg m/s, so Δp = 0 − 12 = −12 kg m/s. F = Δp/t = −12 / 0.5 = −24 N: the force acts opposite to the ball's motion.

questions.stem: If the contact time of a collision doubles while the momentum change stays fixed, the force:

options.explanation: The proportion is inverse, not direct.
The force depends on the time through the division.
Nothing in the equation squares the time.
A fixed momentum change divided by twice the time gives half the force.

questions.stem: Calling force the rate of change of momentum means the force equals the:

options.text: Momentum change multiplied by the time taken
options.explanation: The time divides the change; multiplying is the inverse operation.

options.text: Momentum change on its own, time ignored
options.explanation: A rate always carries a per-time element.

options.text: Momentum change divided by the time taken
options.explanation: Force is how much momentum changes per second of contact.

options.text: Velocity change divided by the object's mass
options.explanation: That mixes unrelated quantities; mass multiplies, it does not divide here.

questions.stem: A racket changes a ball's momentum by 0.5 kg m/s during a 0.1 s hit. The force on the ball is:

options.explanation: That multiplies 0.5 by 0.1 instead of dividing.
That is the force for a 2.0 s contact, not this 0.1 s hit.
That flips the division and computes 0.1 / 0.5.

questions.stem: A 1000 kg car hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds along its original path at 2 m/s after 2 s of contact. Taking the initial direction as positive, the average force on the car is:

options.explanation: It treats the rebound as +2 m/s, giving (2000 − 10000)/2.
Same size but the minus sign was dropped; the force opposes the initial motion.
That divides only the initial momentum (10000 / 2), losing the final-momentum term.

questions.stem: The exam phrase 'inversely proportional' means that when the time for a momentum change shrinks by a factor of 4, the force:

options.explanation: The two quantities move in opposite directions.
A proportional link always responds to the change.
Nothing squares the factor here.
Divide the time by 4 and the force multiplies by 4.

questions.stem: Define force as a rate of change.
questions.modelAnswer: Force is the momentum change per second: the change in momentum divided by the time over which it happens.

questions.stem: State what happens to the force when the time over which a momentum change happens gets shorter.
questions.modelAnswer: The force gets bigger: with the momentum change fixed, a shorter time means dividing by less, and the two quantities are inversely proportional.

questions.stem: Explain why an identical momentum change can produce very different forces in two hits.
questions.modelAnswer: F = Δp/t with the momentum change fixed: dividing by a smaller time gives a larger value. Force and time are inversely proportional, so the shorter contact delivers the bigger force.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg ball strikes a wall at 8 m/s and rebounds along its original path at 2 m/s, touching the wall for 0.25 s. Taking the initial direction as positive, calculate the force on the ball.
questions.modelAnswer: mv = 0.5 × (−2) = −1 kg m/s and mu = 0.5 × 8 = 4 kg m/s, so Δp = −1 − 4 = −5 kg m/s. F = Δp/t = −5 / 0.25 = −20 N: a 20 N force acting opposite to the ball's initial motion.
